claim: Selfish genetic elements can promote their transmission at the expense of individual survival, creating conflict between the element and the rest of the genome.
source: Selfish genetic elements can promote their transmission at the expense of individual survival, creating conflict between the element and the rest of the genome.
evidence: This is a general statement about selfish genetic elements supported by established scientific understanding and citations in the broader context.

claim: A large number of toxin-antidote (TA) post-segregation distorters have been identified in non-obligate outcrossing nematodes.
source: Recently, a large number of toxin-antidote (TA) post-segregation distorters have been identified in non-obligate outcrossing nematodes.
evidence: This statement references recent discoveries in the field, implying citation-based support.

claim: Two major haplotypes of the zeel-1;peel-1 locus, with and without the selfish element, segregate in C. elegans.
source: Two major haplotypes of this locus, with and without the selfish element, segregate in C. elegans.
evidence: This is a factual statement about genetic variation in C. elegans, supported by established knowledge and likely prior studies.

claim: Loss of the toxin peel-1 decreased fitness of hermaphrodites.
source: We evaluate the fitness consequences of the zeel-1;peel-1 element outside of its role in gene drive in non-outcrossing animals and demonstrate that loss of the toxin peel-1 decreased fitness of hermaphrodites and resulted in reductions in fecundity and body size.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Loss of peel-1 resulted in reductions in fecundity.
source: We evaluate the fitness consequences of the zeel-1;peel-1 element outside of its role in gene drive in non-outcrossing animals and demonstrate that loss of the toxin peel-1 decreased fitness of hermaphrodites and resulted in reductions in fecundity and body size.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of fecundity presented in the manuscript.

claim: Loss of peel-1 resulted in reductions in body size.
source: We evaluate the fitness consequences of the zeel-1;peel-1 element outside of its role in gene drive in non-outcrossing animals and demonstrate that loss of the toxin peel-1 decreased fitness of hermaphrodites and resulted in reductions in fecundity and body size.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of body size presented in the manuscript.

claim: peel-1 has a biological role beyond toxin lethality.
source: These findings suggest a biological role for peel-1 beyond toxin lethality.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing fitness effects of peel-1 loss.

claim: A TA element can provide a fitness benefit to its hosts either during their initial evolution or by being co-opted by the animals following their selfish spread.
source: This work demonstrates that a TA element can provide a fitness benefit to its hosts either during their initial evolution or by being co-opted by the animals following their selfish spread.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and theoretical considerations.

claim: Selfish genetic elements are heritable segments of DNA that promote their own transmission relative to the rest of the genome, potentially at the expense of the individual organism.
source: Selfish genetic elements, or selfish genes, are heritable segments of DNA that promote their own transmission relative to the rest of the genome, potentially at the expense of the individual organism (Werren, 2011; Werren et al., 1988).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations to foundational work in the field.

claim: Selfish genetic elements act through a diverse catalog of molecular mechanisms including transposons, homing endonucleases, sex-ratio distorters, and segregation or post-segregation distorters.
source: They act through a diverse catalog of molecular mechanisms to increase their frequency, including transposons, homing endonucleases, sex-ratio distorters, and segregation or post-segregation distorters (Hurst and Werren, 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Selfish genetic elements induce tension between genes and the hosts that carry them, including causing disease and other health problems.
source: Because selfish genetic elements induce tension between genes and the hosts that carry them, including causing disease and other health problems, their discovery and study over the last 50 or so years have motivated major questions—and debate—over the nature and consequences of genetic conflict in inheritance systems (Ågren, 2016; Ågren and Clark, 2018; Hurst and Werren, 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Three outstanding questions about selfish genetic elements are: (i) how they arise, (ii) how they are maintained, and (iii) how they influence evolution.
source: In an early review, and in its revisit 23 years later, Werren, 2011 posed three questions about selfish genetic elements that remain outstanding today: (i) how they arise, (ii) how they are maintained, and (iii) how they influence evolution.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field, supported by a citation.

claim: Theory and observation have indicated that selfish genetic elements decrease in prevalence as inbreeding in a system increases.
source: Theory and observation have indicated that selfish genetic elements decrease in prevalence as inbreeding in a system increases; spreading necessarily requires outcrossing to a vulnerable genetic background (Ågren and Clark, 2018; Hurst and Werren, 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to theoretical and observational work.

claim: Spreading of selfish genetic elements necessarily requires outcrossing to a vulnerable genetic background.
source: Theory and observation have indicated that selfish genetic elements decrease in prevalence as inbreeding in a system increases; spreading necessarily requires outcrossing to a vulnerable genetic background (Ågren and Clark, 2018; Hurst and Werren, 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: A recent wave of discovery of toxin-antidote (TA) elements in non-obligate outcrossing species challenges the view that selfish elements decrease with inbreeding.
source: However, a recent wave of discovery of toxin-antidote (TA) elements in non-obligate outcrossing species (e.g. Ben-David et al., 2017; Ben-David et al., 2021; Noble et al., 2021; Nuckolls et al., 2017; Shen et al., 2017) challenges this view.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to recent discoveries.

claim: TA elements are post-segregation distorters composed of two or more linked sub-elements, including a 'toxin' transmitted cytoplasmically from the parent to the offspring through the gamete and an 'antidote' that rescues when expressed in the zygote.
source: TA elements are post-segregation distorters composed of two or more linked sub-elements, including a 'toxin' transmitted cytoplasmically from the parent to the offspring through the gamete and an 'antidote' that rescues when expressed in the zygote.
evidence: This is a definition of TA elements based on established knowledge.

claim: TA elements induce heavy fitness costs to hybrids heterozygous for an active/inactive genotype because while all gametes will carry the cytoplasmic toxin, only those zygotes that inherit the TA allele will express the antidote and survive.
source: TA elements induce heavy fitness costs to hybrids heterozygous for an active/inactive genotype because while all gametes will carry the cytoplasmic toxin, only those zygotes that inherit the TA allele will express the antidote and survive.
evidence: This is an explanation of the mechanism of TA elements based on established knowledge.

claim: TA systems include Medea elements and functionally similar 'gamete killers'.
source: TA systems, which include Medea elements (e.g. Beeman et al., 1992; Noble et al., 2021) and functionally similar 'gamete killers' (e.g. Nuckolls et al., 2017), have been identified across multiple kingdoms of life, including bacteria, plants, fungi, insects, and nematodes (Akarsu et al., 2019; Bardaji et al., 2019; Beckmann et al., 2017; Beeman et al., 1992; Ben-David et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2008; Leplae et al., 2011; Saavedra De Bast et al., 2008; Seidel et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: TA systems have been identified across multiple kingdoms of life, including bacteria, plants, fungi, insects, and nematodes.

evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: In the nematode genus Caenorhabditis, androdioecy (male and hermaphrodite sexes) has evolved independently three times from a male–female ancestor.
source: In the nematode genus Caenorhabditis, androdioecy (male and hermaphrodite sexes) has evolved independently three times from a male–female ancestor (Ellis, 2017); consequently, C. elegans, C. briggsae, and C. tropicalis reproduce primarily by selfing, with infrequent instances of outcrossing via male mating (Barrière and Félix, 2005; Cutter et al., 2006; Noble et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: C. elegans, C. briggsae, and C. tropicalis reproduce primarily by selfing, with infrequent instances of outcrossing via male mating.

claim: Medea TA elements have been identified in C. elegans, C. briggsae, and C. tropicalis.

evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Multiple Medea TA elements have been identified in both C. elegans and C. tropicalis.

evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The zeel-1;peel-1 locus in C. elegans is one of the most complete mechanistic descriptions of a TA system.
source: One of the most complete mechanistic descriptions of a TA system is the zeel-1;peel-1 locus in C. elegans, in which a sperm-delivered toxin (peel-1) induces arrest in embryos not carrying the zygotically expressed antidote (zeel-1) (Figure 1A; Seidel et al., 2008; Seidel et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In the zeel-1;peel-1 system, a sperm-delivered toxin (peel-1) induces arrest in embryos not carrying the zygotically expressed antidote (zeel-1).

evidence: This statement is supported by citations and a figure showing the mechanism.

claim: The alternative active/inactive haplotypes of zeel-1;peel-1 that segregate within C. elegans exhibit high genetic diversity.

claim: Maintenance of ancient polymorphism in zeel-1;peel-1 is inconsistent with a history of selfish activity.
source: Maintenance (Figure 1C) of ancient polymorphism is inconsistent with a history of selfish activity: in outcrossing populations, genic drive should fix the active haplotype rapidly; in the androdioecious mating system of C. elegans, a high rate of selfing should fix an element at high frequency or allow it to be lost by drift at low frequency (Noble et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference based on theoretical expectations and supported by a citation.

claim: In outcrossing populations, genic drive should fix the active haplotype rapidly.

claim: Under a scenario of no fitness consequence to the host genotype (s = 0) and a completely outcrossing population (k = 1), the zeel-1;peel-1 element spreads rapidly through the population.
source: Under a simple scenario of no fitness consequence to the host genotype (s = 0) and a completely outcrossing population (k = 1), the element spreads rapidly through the population with a maximum allele change comparable to an additive beneficial allele with a selection coefficient of 0.44 (Figure 1E), 2–4 times higher than the selection coefficient of lactase persistence in humans (Bersaglieri et al., 2004).
evidence: This is based on modeling results shown in a figure.

evidence: This is based on experimental fitness data.

claim: Previous work has suggested that TA elements may shape evolution by promoting selfing to escape the cost of selfish gene drive.
source: Previous work has suggested that TA elements may shape evolution by promoting selfing to escape the cost of selfish gene drive (Noble et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: This work provides a mechanism for the spread and maintenance of TA elements that helps to explain their prevalence in selfing Caenorhabditis.
source: Here we provide a mechanism for their spread and maintenance that helps to explain their prevalence in selfing Caenorhabditis (Ben-David et al., 2021; Noble et al., 2021; Sweigart et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and supported by citations.

claim: The observation of a toxin directly affecting biological traits mirrors work in transposable elements, which are also selfish elements that can be domesticated for phenotypic benefit to the organism.
source: Moreover, our observation of a toxin directly affecting biological traits mirrors work in transposable elements, which are also selfish elements that can be domesticated for phenotypic benefit to the organism (Werren, 2011).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work supported by a citation.

claim: This previously undescribed, non-toxin related role of a TA element is expected to shape evolutionary trajectories of both the element and the organism.
source: This previously undescribed, non-toxin related role of a TA element is expected to shape evolutionary trajectories of both the element and the organism.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion about the evolutionary implications of the findings.

claim: peel-1 transcripts are restricted to sperm.
source: peel-1 transcripts are restricted to sperm (Seidel et al., 2011), but these results suggest that it can affect adult phenotypes like fecundity and growth rate.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: peel-1 can affect adult phenotypes like fecundity and growth rate.
source: peel-1 transcripts are restricted to sperm (Seidel et al., 2011), but these results suggest that it can affect adult phenotypes like fecundity and growth rate.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data.

claim: One possibility is that the PEEL-1 protein persists to adulthood and affects cellular function despite its presence at very low levels.
source: One possibility is that the PEEL-1 protein persists to adulthood and affects cellular function despite its presence at very low levels.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the mechanism of peel-1 action.

claim: PEEL-1 may induce long-lasting effects in adulthood via early developmental processes.
source: Alternatively, PEEL-1 may induce long-lasting effects in adulthood via early developmental processes; notably, the toxic effect of PEEL-1 arises late in embryogenesis (Seidel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis supported by a citation about the timing of toxicity.

claim: The toxic effect of PEEL-1 arises late in embryogenesis.
source: Alternatively, PEEL-1 may induce long-lasting effects in adulthood via early developmental processes; notably, the toxic effect of PEEL-1 arises late in embryogenesis (Seidel et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: PEEL-1 may function as a mechanism to communicate parentage to the offspring.
source: As the toxicity of PEEL-1 depends on the sex of the sperm donor, mediated in part by dosage (Seidel et al., 2011), PEEL-1 may function as a mechanism to communicate parentage to the offspring.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on prior work cited.

claim: The toxicity of PEEL-1 depends on the sex of the sperm donor, mediated in part by dosage.
source: As the toxicity of PEEL-1 depends on the sex of the sperm donor, mediated in part by dosage (Seidel et al., 2011), PEEL-1 may function as a mechanism to communicate parentage to the offspring.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: It is possible that environmental conditions of the parent regulate PEEL-1 levels, which could also be communicated to the offspring.
source: Additionally, it is possible that environmental conditions of the parent regulate PEEL-1 levels, which could also be communicated to the offspring.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about potential regulation of PEEL-1.

claim: Two independently derived peel-1 revertant alleles (kah1000, kah1001) restore the original peel-1 mutation (kah126) to wild-type.
source: First, we created two replicate alleles (kah1000 and kah1001) that revert the original peel-1 mutant allele (kah126) back to wild-type.
evidence: This is based on the genetic engineering performed in the study.

claim: Three replicate alleles (kah1003-5) with an edit in the third codon induce an early stop in peel-1.
source: Second, we created three replicate alleles (kah1003-5) with an edit in the third codon to induce an early stop.
evidence: This is based on the genetic engineering performed in the study.

claim: An allele (kah1006) with a 5 bp deletion excised the ATG start codon of peel-1.
source: Finally, we created an allele (kah1006) with a 5 bp deletion that excised the ATG start codon.
evidence: This is based on the genetic engineering performed in the study.

claim: The new peel-1 loss-of-function alleles (kah1003-6) are predicted to create true null alleles that should prevent the production of any peel-1 protein.
source: Unlike the original N2peel-1(trunc) strain, with a stop codon in the third exon that could potentially lead to a truncated protein product, these latter four strains are predicted to create true null alleles that should prevent the production of any peel-1 protein.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic engineering design.

claim: Self-progeny of the heterozygous offspring of the strain with the reversion allele of peel-1 showed 25% lethality.
source: We verified peel-1 activity using embryo killing assays on one strain of each allele type; as expected, self-progeny of the heterozygous offspring of the strain with the reversion allele of peel-1 showed 25% lethality, and self-progeny from crosses with the loss-of-function alleles of peel-1 showed zero lethality (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on experimental embryo lethality assays shown in a figure.

claim: Self-progeny from crosses with the loss-of-function alleles of peel-1 showed zero lethality.
source: We verified peel-1 activity using embryo killing assays on one strain of each allele type; as expected, self-progeny of the heterozygous offspring of the strain with the reversion allele of peel-1 showed 25% lethality, and self-progeny from crosses with the loss-of-function alleles of peel-1 showed zero lethality (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on experimental embryo lethality assays shown in a figure.

claim: Equivalent performance was observed among the replicate genotypes within the reversion and early stop allele classes.
source: We tested these strains in competition experiments and observed equivalent performance among the replicate genotypes within the reversion and early stop allele classes, and further, equivalent performance among all peel-1 mutants (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is based on experimental competition assay data shown in a figure.

claim: Equivalent performance was observed among all peel-1 mutants.
source: We tested these strains in competition experiments and observed equivalent performance among the replicate genotypes within the reversion and early stop allele classes, and further, equivalent performance among all peel-1 mutants (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is based on experimental competition assay data shown in a figure.

claim: Strains carrying the reversion alleles showed no significant difference in fitness in competition with wildtype.
source: As expected, strains carrying the reversion alleles showed no significant difference in fitness in competition with wildtype, while strains carrying the new loss-of-function alleles, like the original N2peel-1(trunc) strain, were significantly outcompeted (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is based on experimental competition assay data shown in a figure.

claim: Strains carrying the new loss-of-function alleles, like the original N2peel-1(trunc) strain, were significantly outcompeted.
source: As expected, strains carrying the reversion alleles showed no significant difference in fitness in competition with wildtype, while strains carrying the new loss-of-function alleles, like the original N2peel-1(trunc) strain, were significantly outcompeted (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is based on experimental competition assay data shown in a figure.

claim: These experiments strongly support a role for peel-1 outside of its role as a selfish element.
source: These experiments strongly support a role for peel-1 outside of its role as a selfish element.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data with multiple alleles.

claim: The phenotypic difference in egg-laying and growth rate could be due to background mutations.
source: We did not test these additional strains to confirm that the egg-laying and growth rate phenotypes that we measured in the original peel-1 loss-of-function, so we cannot exclude the possibility that this phenotypic difference is due to background mutations.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation in the experimental design.

claim: N2zeel-1;peel-1(CB4856) carries an ~140–370 kb interval spanning the zeel-1;peel-1 locus from CB4856 introgressed into N2.
source: First, we employed a previously described fitness assay (Large et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2018) to compete N2zeel-1;peel-1(CB4856), which carries an ~140–370 kb interval spanning the zeel-1;peel-1 locus from CB4856 introgressed into N2 (Ben-David et al., 2017), against N2marker, a modified version of N2 carrying a silent marker mutation in the dpy-10 gene.
evidence: This is a description of the genetic background of a strain used in the study, supported by a citation.

claim: CB4856 harbors the inactive haplotype of zeel-1;peel-1.
source: As CB4856 harbors the inactive haplotype, N2zeel-1;peel-1(CB4856) lacks the toxin/antidote element, while N2marker carries the active element native to N2.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the genetic variation at this locus.
